subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal tubular defects: Fanconi, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, SAME
vignette: A 7-year-old child has growth restriction, rickets, metabolic acidosis, hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and generalized aminoaciduria with glucosuria at normal serum glucose.
question: Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
explanation_correct: Fanconi syndrome is a generalized proximal tubular reabsorption defect causing excretion of amino acids, glucose, HCO3-, and PO4(3-). Bicarbonate loss causes proximal (type 2) RTA with metabolic acidosis; phosphate wasting causes hypophosphatemia, rickets/osteopenia, and growth restriction; volume depletion and hypokalemia are common. Causes include Wilson disease, tyrosinemia, glycogen storage disease, myeloma, ischemia, and drugs (ifosfamide, cisplatin, tenofovir, lead).

explanation_incorrect.A: Bartter syndrome is a thick ascending limb defect causing metabolic alkalosis, hypokalemia, and hypercalciuria, not acidosis or aminoaciduria.
explanation_incorrect.B: Gitelman syndrome is a distal NaCl defect causing alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and hypokalemia, not proximal wasting or acidosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Liddle syndrome causes hypertension, hypokalemia, alkalosis, and low aldosterone, not rickets or aminoaciduria.
explanation_incorrect.E: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension, hypokalemia, and alkalosis, not generalized proximal tubular wasting.

educationalObjective: Fanconi syndrome is generalized proximal tubular dysfunction causing aminoaciduria, glucosuria, phosphaturia, bicarbonate loss (proximal RTA), and rickets.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal tubular defects: Fanconi, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, SAME
vignette: A young child with failure to thrive is found to have Fanconi syndrome. Genetic testing reveals a defect in copper metabolism with hepatolenticular degeneration.
question: Which of the following is a recognized cause of Fanconi syndrome?
explanation_correct: Wilson disease (copper accumulation) is a classic hereditary cause of Fanconi syndrome, along with tyrosinemia and glycogen storage disease. Other causes include ischemia, multiple myeloma, and drugs or toxins such as ifosfamide, cisplatin, tenofovir, and lead poisoning, all of which injure the proximal tubule.

explanation_incorrect.B: Primary hyperaldosteronism is an adrenal steroid excess state causing hypertension and hypokalemia, not proximal tubular injury.
explanation_incorrect.C: Liddle syndrome is a genetic Na+ channel gain-of-function in the collecting duct causing hypertension, not Fanconi syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: SAME (apparent mineralocorticoid excess) is due to 11-beta-HSD deficiency or licorice and does not cause proximal tubular wasting.
explanation_incorrect.E: A renin-secreting tumor causes secondary hyperaldosteronism and hypertension, not generalized proximal tubule dysfunction.

educationalObjective: Wilson disease is a classic cause of Fanconi syndrome; other causes include myeloma, ischemia, and nephrotoxic drugs.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal tubular defects: Fanconi, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, SAME
vignette: A teenager has muscle cramps, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypochloremia, and hypercalciuria. Blood pressure is normal. Genetic testing shows an autosomal recessive disorder of the thick ascending limb.
question: Which diagnosis is most likely?
explanation_correct: Bartter syndrome is an autosomal recessive defect in the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter of the thick ascending limb, producing a loop-diuretic-like picture: metabolic alkalosis, hypochloremia, hypokalemia, and hypercalciuria with normal blood pressure. It presents similarly to chronic loop diuretic use.

explanation_incorrect.A: Gitelman syndrome affects the distal Na/Cl cotransporter and features hypomagnesemia and low urine calcium, distinguishing it from Bartter.
explanation_incorrect.B: Liddle syndrome features hypertension and low aldosterone due to increased collecting duct Na+ reabsorption, not a thick ascending limb defect.
explanation_incorrect.D: SAME (apparent mineralocorticoid excess) causes hypertension with low aldosterone from mineralocorticoid receptor activation by cortisol.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fanconi syndrome is a proximal tubular defect causing metabolic acidosis and aminoaciduria, not alkalosis or hypercalciuria.

educationalObjective: Bartter syndrome is an AR thick ascending limb Na/K/2Cl defect causing alkalosis, hypokalemia, hypercalciuria, and normal BP (like a loop diuretic).

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal tubular defects: Fanconi, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, SAME
vignette: An adult has hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and low urinary calcium. Blood pressure is normal, and the disorder is less severe than a similar thick ascending limb disorder.
question: Which diagnosis fits this thiazide-like picture?
explanation_correct: Gitelman syndrome is an autosomal recessive defect in the distal convoluted tubule Na+/Cl- cotransporter, producing a chronic-thiazide-like picture: metabolic alkalosis, hypochloremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and low urine calcium. It is generally less severe than Bartter syndrome. The hypomagnesemia and low urine Ca2+ distinguish it from Bartter.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bartter syndrome (thick ascending limb defect) has normal magnesium and high urine calcium, not hypomagnesemia and low urine calcium.
explanation_incorrect.C: Liddle syndrome is a gain-of-function Na+ channel mutation with hypertension and suppressed aldosterone, not a distal NaCl defect.
explanation_incorrect.D: SAME is due to impaired cortisol inactivation (11-beta-HSD deficiency) causing hypertension with low aldosterone.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fanconi syndrome is a proximal defect causing acidosis, hypophosphatemia, and aminoaciduria, not alkalosis or hypomagnesemia.

educationalObjective: Gitelman syndrome is an AR distal NaCl defect causing a thiazide-like alkalosis, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and low urine Ca2+.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal tubular defects: Fanconi, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, SAME
vignette: Two patients present with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and normal blood pressure. Patient 1 has hypercalciuria and normal serum magnesium; Patient 2 has hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria.
question: Which combination of findings correctly distinguishes Bartter from Gitelman syndrome?

options.text: Bartter: hypomagnesemia and low urine Ca2+; Gitelman: normal Mg and high urine Ca2+
Both have hypomagnesemia, but only Bartter has metabolic alkalosis
Bartter is due to a distal tubule defect; Gitelman is due to a thick ascending limb defect
Gitelman has high urine Ca2+; Bartter has low urine Ca2+
Bartter: high urine Ca2+ and normal Mg (loop-like); Gitelman: low Mg and low urine Ca2+ (thiazide-like)

explanation_correct: Bartter syndrome (thick ascending limb Na/K/2Cl defect) mimics chronic loop diuretic use: alkalosis, hypokalemia, hypercalciuria, and normal magnesium. Gitelman syndrome (distal NaCl defect) mimics chronic thiazide use: alkalosis, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalciuria. Both have high renin and aldosterone with normal blood pressure; magnesium and urine calcium differentiate them.

explanation_incorrect.A: This reverses the findings; Bartter has normal Mg and high urine Ca2+, while Gitelman has low Mg and low urine Ca2+.
explanation_incorrect.B: Both cause metabolic alkalosis; hypomagnesemia is characteristic of Gitelman, not Bartter.
explanation_incorrect.C: The segments are reversed: Bartter is a thick ascending limb defect and Gitelman is a distal convoluted tubule defect.
explanation_incorrect.D: This reverses urine calcium: Bartter has high urine Ca2+ and Gitelman has low urine Ca2+.

educationalObjective: Bartter (loop-like) has high urine Ca2+ with normal Mg; Gitelman (thiazide-like) has low Mg and low urine Ca2+.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal tubular defects: Fanconi, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, SAME
vignette: A young boy has severe hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and nearly undetectable serum aldosterone. His father had similar findings in adolescence. Genetic testing shows an autosomal dominant condition.
question: Which diagnosis and treatment pairing is correct?

options.text: Gitelman syndrome; treatment with magnesium supplementation

explanation_correct: Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutation that decreases degradation of the collecting duct Na+ channel (ENaC), increasing Na+ reabsorption. It mimics hyperaldosteronism with hypertension, hypokalemia, and alkalosis, but aldosterone is nearly undetectable. Treatment is amiloride (or triamterene), which blocks ENaC directly.

explanation_incorrect.A: Gitelman syndrome is autosomal recessive and normotensive with hypomagnesemia; magnesium supplementation would not address this hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bartter syndrome is autosomal recessive and normotensive with hypercalciuria, not dominant hypertension with suppressed aldosterone.
explanation_incorrect.C: Primary hyperaldosteronism has high (not undetectable) aldosterone and low renin; adrenalectomy is not indicated here.
explanation_incorrect.E: SAME is autosomal recessive and due to 11-beta-HSD deficiency; the autosomal dominant family history and near-absent aldosterone with ENaC gain-of-function point to Liddle, treated with amiloride.

educationalObjective: Liddle syndrome is AD ENaC gain-of-function causing hypertension with suppressed aldosterone; amiloride is the treatment.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal tubular defects: Fanconi, Bartter, Gitelman, Liddle, SAME
vignette: A patient has hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis with very low aldosterone. The disorder can be inherited via 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency or acquired by consuming large amounts of licorice.
question: Which mechanism best explains the mineralocorticoid excess in syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess (SAME)?

options.text: Cortisol activates mineralocorticoid receptors because 11-beta-HSD normally inactivates cortisol to cortisone; deficiency or licorice (glycyrrhetinic acid) blocks this inactivation
Aldosterone is overproduced by an adrenal adenoma
ENaC degradation is decreased by a gain-of-function mutation
Renin secretion is increased by a juxtaglomerular cell tumor
The Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb is overactive

explanation_correct: Normally 11-beta-HSD converts cortisol to cortisone, which is inactive at mineralocorticoid receptors. In hereditary 11-beta-HSD deficiency (autosomal recessive) or after licorice ingestion (glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits the enzyme), cortisol accumulates and activates mineralocorticoid receptors, causing Na+ retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, alkalosis, and suppressed aldosterone. Treatment is K+-sparing diuretics or exogenous corticosteroids to suppress endogenous cortisol.

explanation_incorrect.B: Aldosterone is suppressed in SAME; an adenoma would cause primary hyperaldosteronism with high aldosterone, not SAME.
explanation_incorrect.C: Decreased ENaC degradation is the mechanism of Liddle syndrome, not SAME.
explanation_incorrect.D: Increased renin from a juxtaglomerular cell tumor would raise aldosterone; SAME has suppressed renin and aldosterone.
explanation_incorrect.E: Thick ascending limb Na/K/2Cl overactivity is not the mechanism; SAME acts via renal mineralocorticoid receptor activation by cortisol.

educationalObjective: SAME results from cortisol activating mineralocorticoid receptors when 11-beta-HSD is deficient or inhibited by licorice, with low aldosterone.
